extracted.intended_audience: regulatory professionals, agency staff, attorneys, trainees, and members of the public seeking an overview of notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for conducting informal (APA §553) notice-and-comment rulemaking, including required procedural steps, who may participate, and agency discretion over hearings and hearing format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish an NPRM in the Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing an NPRM in the Federal Register is the first step of informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per the APA's informal rulemaking procedures, the process 'in its most simple form, involves: (1) publishing an NPRM in the Federal Register; ...' — agencies must publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to begin the notice-and-comment process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Inviting public comment on the proposed rule (the second step of the process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM must include an opportunity for public comment; the process is often called 'notice-and-comment rulemaking' because inviting and receiving comments is a central procedural element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider the public comments submitted in response to the NPRM (the third step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must actually consider the comments before issuing a final rule; consideration of comments is a core procedural requirement of notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish a final rule in the Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: After considering comments, the agency publishes a final rule in the Federal Register (the fourth step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule publication completes the informal rulemaking sequence described by the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may participate — 'interested person' may submit comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, any 'interested person' may submit comments in an informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each informal rulemaking action 'has the potential to be like a national town hall meeting; anyone who wants to may participate.' This underscores broad standing to participate in notice-and-comment proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to hold oral hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency has discretion whether or not to hold an oral hearing during informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the APA leaves hearings to agency discretion, an agency's own statute sometimes requires hearings in certain matters (see hybrid rulemaking). The agency decides whether a hearing is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to set hearing ground rules and format
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency holds a hearing, it has discretion to set the ground rules and determine the hearing format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearings may range from very informal 'legislative-like' sessions where people read or state views for the record, to very formal proceedings with sworn witnesses and cross-examination; the agency sets procedural bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal rulemaking should be a legislative-like opportunity for public influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal rulemaking is intended to be a legislative-like process in which the rulemaker gives the public an opportunity to influence regulatory decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy to a legislator and a 'national town hall meeting' suggests the principle that informal rulemaking procedures should meaningfully enable public input and influence on rule content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish informal rulemaking from formal (trial-type) rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal (notice-and-comment) rulemaking is distinct from formal, trial-type rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal rulemaking is rarely used; agencies should be aware of the procedural and evidentiary differences between informal and formal rulemaking and apply the appropriate process (see Formal Rulemaking).
